name: Wendy Rossi

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Wendy. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Is that all right?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Fine by me. I'm Wendy, 27, and I'm an apprentice lineworker with the regional electricity company, about eighteen months in. I live on my own with my dog, Biscuit, in a small rented house on the edge of town.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Good. Then let's start simple. Walk me through a normal working day for you.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: We're the pole replacement crew, so mostly we swap out rotten wooden poles and clear trees and brush away from the lines along the back roads. I drive the truck to site, set out the cones, dig, run the winch, and do whatever Stan Briggs, my foreman, tells me. He's old school, which suits me. I eat lunch in the cab with Kev, who's been doing this 30 years and tells me everything that's ever gone wrong.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What did you do before this?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Six years on the checkouts at the supermarket on the high street. Then they put in the self-checkout machines and cut our hours to nothing. I picked line work because you can't do it from a screen, and I still write everything in a paper notebook in my vest pocket.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. That's what I'd hope for, to be honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's what I expected: a lot of noise for nothing much. I'd say it at lunch to Kev and leave it there. I don't post things online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means I keep doing what I came here to do. My work is digging, winching and climbing, so a computer saving the office a bit of time doesn't touch me. I'd be happy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep turning up and keep learning off Stan and Kev. I'd pay extra on my truck loan so it's gone in two years instead of three. And I'd try to get back to three months of bills saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Relieved, really. Like when the forecast says the storm's going to miss us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the self-checkouts pushed you out. Does that still sit with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, a bit. I left the supermarket checkout because a machine was coming for it. I picked this trade so I'd never have to think about computers again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Leaving AI aside, is anything already pressing on your money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The truck loan, mainly, about 340 a month. I've got about two months of bills saved, which is fine, but my landlord's selling up next year and I'll have to find somewhere else.

say: AI was **a lot of noise** for nothing much.
I'd say that at lunch to Kev and **leave it** there, not online.
think: My work is **digging and winching**, so office time savings don't touch me.
This is the world I **picked this trade** for.
do: Overpay the **truck loan** so it's cleared in two years, not three.
Build savings back to **three months** of bills.
Keep learning the trade from foreman **Stan** and old hand Kev.
feel: **Relieved**, like a storm forecast that says it will miss town.
S0.quote: I left the supermarket checkout because a machine was coming for it. I picked this trade so I'd never have to think about computers again.
fieldNote: Her choice of trade was a **reaction** to self-checkouts taking her old job.
Pressures are the **truck loan** and a landlord selling up, but she feels secure.
She never posts online and keeps a **paper notebook**, a clear sign of resistance to tech.

steps.text: Keep learning pole replacement from Stan and Kev
Overpay the 340 a month truck loan to clear it early

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hm. That sounds like what they did at the supermarket, just slower.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the office can have their robots, out here it's still a shovel and a winch. I'd moan about it with Kev. I wouldn't say much else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the company wants me on a tablet, I'll use the tablet. I just won't pretend I like it, and I'll keep my paper notebook in my vest. My actual work is safe; it's the paperwork and the dispatch people that change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the training they make me do and nothing extra. I'd keep paying off the truck and wait to see if any of it sticks. I'm not changing anything until I have to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's on my mind because I've seen this film before, but I don't think it's coming for my job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would you notice it first on your crew?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The job packets. Right now a planner called Sue prints them and we get them from Stan. In this picture it'd come on a screen from a computer, and Sue would be gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You say it won't touch you, but you sound tense. Which is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both, I suppose. I believe my job's fine. But I said that at the supermarket too, so part of me doesn't trust myself.

say: The office can have **their robots**; out here it's a shovel and a winch.
I'd moan about it with **Kev** at lunch and leave it.
think: I'll use the **tablet** if made to, but keep my paper notebook.
My work is safe; **paperwork and dispatch** are what change.
do: Do the **required training** and nothing extra.
Keep paying off the **truck** and wait to see what sticks.
feel: **Uneasy**, because she believed her **old job** was safe too.
S1.quote: If the company wants me on a tablet, I'll use the tablet. I just won't pretend I like it, and I'll keep my paper notebook in my vest.
fieldNote: She would comply with **new tools** but go no further than required.
The planner Sue's **printed packets** stand for the office work she sees going.
She names her own **distrust** of herself, a lesson from the supermarket.

steps.text: Do only the required tablet training for job packets
Wait a year to see which new systems actually stick

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Oh. No. That's fast. That's really fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say someone needs to slow this down, and I don't much care who, the government or the companies. I'd say it to anyone who'd listen. I still wouldn't post it, but I'd say it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 31 when the robots come, still paying for my truck, with half a trade and no plan B. Pole work isn't that clever; a robot that can dig and lift would do most of what I do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut everything: no takeaways, no new boots till the old ones die, sell my quad bike for about 2,000. I'd put all of it into savings and clear the truck loan. Then I'd ring my brother Rob, who runs a small digging business, and ask if he'd keep a spot for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. It's the supermarket all over again, but this time I'd have nowhere to run to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The card says robots come about three years after the thinking AI. What happens to you in those three years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2028 the office goes, so Stan gets his orders from a computer and probably so do I. I'd keep working, but I'd know there's a date on it. I'd lie awake doing the sums on the truck and the rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you turn to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rob, and my mum. Rob's diggers would get robots too, eventually, but small firms are slower. And Mum would have a room if it came to that, which I'd hate.

say: Someone needs to **slow this down**, government or companies, I don't care which.
I'd say it out loud to anyone, though **still not online**.
think: I'd be **31** with half a trade and no plan B.
A robot that can **dig and lift** would do most of my job.
do: Sell the **quad bike** for about 2,000 and put it into savings.
Cut **takeaways and new gear** and clear the truck loan.
Ask my brother **Rob** to keep a spot at his digging business.
feel: **Alarmed**, like the supermarket again with **nowhere to run**.
S2.quote: I'd be 31 when the robots come, still paying for my truck, with half a trade and no plan B.
fieldNote: She sees her **pole work** as routine enough for early robots.
Her plan is all **cutting and family**, with no retraining at all.
The **three-year gap** feels like a countdown, not a chance.

steps.text: Sell the quad bike for about 2,000
Put all spare money into clearing the truck loan
Ask brother Rob to hold a spot at his digging firm

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Better. Not much better, but better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time for the company to look after its people if it wants to. I'd ask Stan what the union and the bosses are planning. That's about all I'd say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is long enough to tell myself it isn't coming. I know myself, and I'd waste the first three. I'd qualify, earn proper money for a bit, and then robots in 2034 would still catch me at 35.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the apprenticeship and put the extra money from qualifying into savings, maybe 300 a month. I'd pay off the truck. Beyond that, honestly, I'd wait to see what the company does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicking, but it'd be there at the back of everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Saving, mostly. With full pay from 2028 I could get six months of bills put away. That's the only thing I'd trust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd waste the first three years. Why say that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it's what I did at the supermarket. They put one self-checkout in as a trial, and I told myself it'd fail. Two years later there were twelve.

say: There's time for the company to **look after** its people if it wants to.
I'd ask Stan what the **union and bosses** are planning.
think: I'd **waste three years** telling myself it isn't coming.
Robots in **2034** would still catch me at 35.
do: Finish the **apprenticeship** and save the qualified pay rise.
Put about **300 a month** away toward six months of bills.
Wait to see what the **company** offers before changing anything.
feel: **Anxious**, sitting at the back of everything without panic.
S3.quote: Five years is long enough to tell myself it isn't coming. I know myself, and I'd waste the first three.
fieldNote: Remarkably **self-aware** about her own tendency to deny change.
The **self-checkout trial** story explains her distrust of slow warnings.
Her only active step is **saving**; everything else waits on the company.

steps.text: Finish the apprenticeship and keep working the pole crew
Save about 300 a month from the qualified pay rise
Wait for the company's plan before changing anything

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years? I'd be nearly 40 when the robots come. That's a different thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time and lots can change. I'd tell people not to panic. That's what Kev would say too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is too far away for me to lose sleep over. I'll worry about 2039 when my knees start worrying me. By then I'd be a proper lineworker with a decade in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as normal: qualify, pay off the truck, maybe put down a deposit on a little house. I wouldn't change trades. I'd watch what the company does and decide later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but only a bit. It's something on the horizon, not on the doorstep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be 40 with most of a career still ahead. Doesn't that worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It does, if I think about it properly. But I'd have a decade of skill by then, and I'd hope that counts for something. I'd be the one who knows what a rotten pole sounds like when you hit it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you do anything different, knowing it's coming?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not, if I'm honest. I'd keep saving, which I'd do anyway. I'm not someone who changes before she has to.

say: Ten years is **a long time**, and lots can change.
I'd tell people **not to panic**, same as Kev would.
think: **2039** is too far away to lose sleep over.
A **decade of skill** should count for something when robots arrive.
do: Qualify, clear the **truck loan** and keep the same crew.
Put down a **deposit** on a small house if savings allow.
Watch the company's moves and **decide later** about anything bigger.
feel: **Uneasy**, but only a little, like weather on the **horizon**.
S4.quote: Ten years is too far away for me to lose sleep over. I'll worry about 2039 when my knees start worrying me.
fieldNote: Long warning makes her **relax**, the opposite of what time to prepare is for.
She hopes **experience** will protect her but admits she won't act early.
Her plan is the same as normal life: **qualify, pay off, buy**.

steps.text: Qualify and stay on the pole replacement crew
Watch the company's robot plans before changing trades

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. I took this job because nobody can do it from a laptop. Now everyone tells me a robot can do it from a truck. What would help is the company telling us straight what it's planning, and some kind of guarantee for people already on the crews.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about people like me who already got moved on once. You don't trust anyone's promises the second time around.

headlineQuote: I took this job because nobody can do it from a laptop. Now everyone tells me a robot can do it from a truck.
portrait: Wendy is a 27-year-old **apprentice** on a pole replacement crew, living alone with her dog.
She left a **supermarket checkout** job after self-checkouts cut her hours, and chose line work to avoid computers.
She never uses **AI tools** and keeps a paper notebook in her vest.
She is calm in a plateau but **alarmed** at AGI by 2028, with no plan beyond cutting back.
Longer warnings make her **relax**, which she admits is how she lost out last time.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, which would catch her at 31 with half a trade.
whatWouldHelp: The company telling crews **straight** what it is planning.
A **guarantee** for people already working on the crews.
